evidence: Ter. Ph. 548: in ignōtum hinc abdūcet locum
Liv. 28.44.3: major ignōtārum rērum est terror
terms.comment: A strange place or person is one we do not know: locus ignōtus, homō ignōtus. In poetry it can also mean lowborn (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Aug. Civ. 19.7: quam cum homine aliēnō
terms.comment: Above all “someone else’s” (aliēnum aes, debt; domus aliēna, another’s house); so a stranger, an outsider; also “unsuited to” and “unfriendly” (Lewis & Short). For a foreigner see foreign.

phrases.latin: Alius ab oculīs meīs illam in ignōtum hinc abdūcet locum? Hem!
phrases.english: Is another man to take her out of my sight from here to some strange place? What!
what we don’t know frightens us more

phrases.latin: ita ut libentius homō sit cum cane suō quam cum homine aliēnō
phrases.english: so that a man would rather be with his own dog than with a stranger

sources: Lewis & Short: ignotus · Lewis & Short: alienus
